metadata.note: Six historical, now-discontinued railroads that served Denver, CO before RTD's modern rail network (see data/rtd_denver.geojson and data/rtd_denver_light_rail.geojson), researched from Wikipedia and railroad-history sites in response to a question about why 1930s Denver showed no rail at all: the Denver Pacific Railway and Kansas Pacific Railway (the two railroads that put Denver on the map in 1870, absorbed into Union Pacific in 1880), the Denver & Rio Grande Railway (Colorado's iconic mountain railroad, here just its original 1871-72 Denver-Pueblo main line), and three of the interurban/streetcar systems that were Denver's actual local transit before RTD -- Denver Tramway's core network, its Denver & Intermountain subsidiary to Golden, and the independent Denver & Interurban Railroad to Boulder. All predate any GTFS/live-data era and have no modern segment (none of these routes carry passenger rail today, though Union Pacific still runs freight on former Denver Pacific/Kansas Pacific trackage and RTD's own commuter/light rail now serves some of the same corridors on new alignments). Route geometry follows the real intermediate towns each railroad's own history describes, but is a simplified handful of waypoints, not surveyed track centerline. Era boundaries follow real corporate-history milestones (line openings, mergers, bankruptcy/discontinuation dates); headway_min and avg_speed_kmh within each era are estimates, not sourced from real timetables.
metadata.source: Wikipedia, american-rails.com, coloradoencyclopedia.org, utahrails.net, denverurbanism.com (see conversation for citations)
metadata.horsecar_audit: 2026-08-24: reviewed in a repo-wide horsecar audit and LEFT UNCHANGED as an unresolved borderline. The denver-tramway-broadway 1886-1888 segment opened under an electrified third rail and, per its own note, 'after a lossmaking year the company reverted to horse-drawn cars' before going to cable in the late 1880s. The segment therefore covers both electric and animal haulage, and no date has been found for the reversion, so it could not be split cleanly. Anyone who finds that date should trim the animal-powered part. REPO RULE 5: this map shows MECHANICALLY powered rail -- horsecars and mule cars are out of scope, and a line's drawn years must start when it stopped using animals. Notes may still mention the animal era as context. See CLAUDE.md.
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.
metadata.interurban_audit: 2026-08-24: features on this layer that are inter-city electric railways were retagged mode='interurban' (previously 'streetcar' or 'intercity_rail') so the map can draw them distinctly from city streetcars and from steam roads. See CLAUDE.md Rule 7.

segments.note: D&RGW took formal control Aug 1, 1921 after the D&RG's bankruptcy reorganization -- a genuine ownership change (old D&RG stockholders received nothing), so this feature is colored separately from the preceding D&RG era. Standard-gauged and by now Colorado's dominant mountain railroad, Denver-Pueblo remained a core Rio Grande passenger corridor for decades, latterly served by trains such as the Royal Gorge. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable

Through Denver-Pueblo passenger service ended in 1964 when the Royal Gorge was cut back to run only as far as Salida; the Colorado Public Utilities Commission allowed the Rio Grande to drop the train entirely, with the last Denver-Salida run on July 27 1967. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable
